lines: Duplicate a file descriptor with a real system call, then read from the original and then from the duplicate.
Does the duplicate start reading from the beginning of the file, or from wherever the original left off?
answer: It continues from exactly where the original stopped.
Both descriptors point at the same open file description underneath, and that description is where the real offset actually lives.

lines: Run it for real: the original descriptor reads the first half of the file, and the duplicate reads exactly the second half.
Continuing from the shared offset, never restarting from the beginning.
Drop an owned file descriptor, and a moment later try a raw system call on that exact same descriptor number.
What happens?
answer: It fails outright. The descriptor is genuinely gone.
That's the entire point of an owned descriptor: dropping it closes the real resource underneath, not just a number.

lines: Run it for real: after the owned descriptor was dropped, a raw call on its number failed outright, exactly as it should.
And a borrowed descriptor, taken from a completely different file that was never dropped, stayed valid the entire time.
steps.takeaway: Dropping an owned file descriptor genuinely closes it — a raw call on that number afterward fails outright.

lines: Open the same file twice — once the normal way, once with its close-on-exec flag explicitly cleared — then fork and exec a genuinely real child process.
Which file descriptor is still open inside that child?
answer: Only the one with close-on-exec explicitly cleared.
The normally-opened one was never going to survive into the child in the first place.

lines: Run it for real: the descriptor that was opened normally never appeared inside the real, forked child at all.
The one with close-on-exec explicitly cleared leaked straight into it, exactly as cleared.
steps.takeaway: A file descriptor closes on exec by default — that genuinely stops it leaking into a forked child.

lines: So step back: why does any of this matter for a real, long-running service?
Can it just keep opening file descriptors, forever?
answer: No — a real kernel limit genuinely caps how many it may hold open at once.
Every descriptor counts against that same ceiling, whether it was duplicated, leaked, or opened the ordinary way.

lines: That real ceiling is defined as one more than the highest file descriptor number a process is ever allowed to have open.
Try to open past it, and the attempt fails outright — not eventually, not gracefully. Outright.
So, pulling this together: every one of these behaviors exists for the same reason.
A file descriptor is a handle into a kernel resource, never the resource itself — so duplicating it, closing it, and leaking it are each their own, completely separate event.
steps.takeaway: A file descriptor is a handle, not the resource itself — closing or leaking it are separate, real events.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: duplicating a descriptor never gives it its own offset — the two stay tied to one real position, together.
Dropping an owned descriptor closes the real resource underneath, something a mere borrow is never able to do.
And whether a descriptor survives into a forked child comes down to one flag, set by default for exactly this reason.
